title: Web Crawler
prompt: Design a polite, deduplicating web crawler at internet scale. Given a seed list, the crawler should fetch and store the HTML of every reachable page on the public web. Target ~1B pages crawled per month, respecting robots.txt and per-domain rate limits.

stages.title: Functional Requirements
stages.questionPrompt: What are the core functional requirements?
stages.howToAnswer: Fetch HTML, extract links, store, recur. Respect robots.txt. Don't drift into search indexing or ranking.

must: Fetch HTML for a given URL
Discover new URLs from fetched pages
Respect robots.txt and per-domain rate limits
should: Avoid re-crawling unchanged pages too often
avoid: Designing the search index — that's a different system

stages.sampleAnswer:
1. Given a URL, fetch the HTML and store it.
2. Extract outbound links from each fetched page and enqueue them.
3. Respect robots.txt and per-domain crawl-delay rules.
4. Avoid fetching the same URL twice within a refresh window.
5. Detect near-duplicate content and skip storing it twice.
hints: What does the crawler do with each URL? Three core actions, plus a control-plane action.
Politeness is a user-visible (well, host-visible) requirement, not just an NFR. What does it look like in practice?
Don't drift into ranking, indexing, or search — that's a different system.

stages.title: Non-Functional Requirements
stages.howToAnswer: Throughput, politeness, fault tolerance, storage scale, freshness. Quantify.

must: Fault tolerance — single fetcher failure must not lose URLs
should: Freshness target — recrawl interval per content type
Extensibility for new content types (RSS, sitemaps)
avoid: Forgetting politeness — the most common failure mode of bad crawler designs
Promising consistency on a globally-distributed crawl frontier

stages.sampleAnswer:
- Throughput: ~400 pages/sec sustained (1B / 30d ≈ 386).
- Politeness: max 1 concurrent request per host, default 1 req/sec unless robots.txt specifies otherwise.
- Fault tolerance: any single fetcher / parser failure does not lose URLs in flight.
- Storage: avg 100KB/page → ~100TB/month, ~1.2PB/year.
- Freshness: news domains recrawled daily; long-tail every 30 days.
- Eventual consistency on the URL frontier is fine.
hints: Quantify pages/sec, total pages, and total bytes. The numbers determine whether your design is feasible.
Politeness, freshness, and dedupe are correctness NFRs — each gets a concrete target.
Cost matters at this scale. What's the egress / storage envelope you'd target?

stages.title: Core Entities
stages.howToAnswer: URL, Page (the fetched content), Frontier (the queue), HostPolicy.

avoid: Mixing the queue and the storage as one entity

stages.sampleAnswer:
- URL: { url, priority, discoveredAt, lastFetchedAt? }
- Frontier: priority queue of URLs to fetch, partitioned by host.
- HostPolicy: cached robots.txt + crawl-delay per host.
- Page: { url, fetchedAt, status, contentHash, html }.
- LinkGraph: outbound links extracted, used to rediscover.
hints: Three big nouns: the work queue, the artifact, and the host-level state. Name them.
Bloom-filter-friendly entities are key — what's the seen-set entity?

stages.title: API
stages.howToAnswer: Crawler is mostly internal — there's an admin API for seeds and metrics, plus internal queues. Don't over-spec REST.

must: Internal queue protocol described (even if not REST)
avoid: Inventing user-facing APIs the system doesn't need

hints: There's barely a public API. The interesting interfaces are the internal queues / topics — what flows through each?
Operators need control: seeding URLs, adjusting per-host policy, and observing health.

stages.title: High-Level Design
stages.questionPrompt: Sketch the components and walk through the fetch path.
stages.howToAnswer: Frontier → fetcher pool → parser → URL filter → dedupe → storage. Show how host politeness is enforced. Show the recursive discovery loop.

must: Distributed frontier partitioned by host (so politeness is local to one worker)
Fetcher pool that respects per-host rate limit
Dedupe before re-enqueue (URL seen-before? content seen-before?)
should: Bloom filter for cheap URL-seen check
avoid: Single-process queue that doesn't scale horizontally

stages.sampleAnswer:
Frontier: Kafka topic, partitioned by host hash → each fetcher consumer is responsible for a stable subset of hosts. This is the key trick — it means politeness can be enforced in-process without distributed locks.

Fetcher pool (1000s of stateless workers): for each URL, check the in-memory robots.txt cache (refresh every 24h). Apply the host crawl-delay (sleep if needed). Fetch via HTTP client with timeouts. Publish 'page fetched' event with raw HTML to a Kafka topic.

Parser (separate worker pool): consumes 'page fetched' events. Extracts outbound links. Normalizes URLs (strip fragments, canonical case, sort query params). Publishes 'link discovered' events.

URL filter: dedupe via a sharded Bloom filter — if probably-seen, drop. Otherwise compute hash, check authoritative seen-set in a sharded KV store, write-through, enqueue back into the frontier.

Content dedupe: SHA-256 of normalized HTML. If we've already stored a page with this hash, just record the additional URL pointing at it.

Storage: HTML compressed and written to S3 (one object per page, keyed by content hash). Metadata in Cassandra keyed by URL.
hints: The headline trick is how you enforce per-host politeness across thousands of workers without distributed locks. What's the partitioning?
After fetch, separate the fetch step from the parse step. Why?
Dedupe twice: at the URL level (cheap pre-filter + authoritative seen-set) and at the content level (hash). Why both?

deepDives.title: Per-host politeness at scale
deepDives.questionPrompt: How do you guarantee no host receives more than its crawl-delay-rate of requests, even with thousands of fetcher workers?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: Partition the frontier by hash(host) into N Kafka partitions; each fetcher worker consumes a stable subset. Within a worker, host politeness is just an in-memory delay queue — no locks, no Redis. Big hosts (say, en.wikipedia.org) get their own dedicated partition via a hot-host override map so a single worker doesn't bottleneck. Rebalancing on worker scale-out uses sticky partition assignment so the in-memory robots.txt and last-fetched-at caches stay warm.

avoid: Global rate limiter at scale (becomes the bottleneck)
Workers picking arbitrary URLs without host affinity

hints: If two workers fetch the same host in parallel, you've broken politeness. How do you guarantee they don't?
What does a global rate limiter cost you at scale? Why does host-affinity sidestep that?
Hot hosts (Wikipedia, GitHub) are problematic — what's the override?

deepDives.title: URL and content dedupe
deepDives.questionPrompt: How do you avoid re-fetching the same URL — or storing the same page twice when it's reachable from multiple URLs?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: Canonicalize URLs first: lowercase host, strip default port and fragment, sort query params, drop tracking params. Then a sharded Bloom filter (per-host shard) gives a cheap probably-seen check; on probably-seen, hit the authoritative seen-set in a sharded KV (Cassandra) to confirm. False positives in Bloom are tolerable — you just skip a URL that may be new (acceptable for a recrawl). For content, hash the parsed/normalized HTML; if the hash is already stored, append a URL→hash mapping instead of writing a duplicate object.

avoid: String-equality URL dedupe with no canonicalization
Storing each URL's HTML even when the content is identical

hints: Canonicalize first. What URL transformations turn 'visually different' into 'logically identical'?
Why use a Bloom filter as a pre-filter? What's tolerable about its false-positive rate here?
Content dedupe operates on the parsed bytes. What's the right hash, and what do you store on a hit?

deepDives.title: Fetch failures and traps
deepDives.questionPrompt: What happens when a host is slow, down, or returns a never-ending crawl trap (calendars, infinite pagination)?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: Per-URL: bounded retries with exponential backoff on 5xx and timeouts; permanent skip on 4xx. Per-host: a circuit breaker — if the rolling error rate crosses a threshold, demote the host to a slower partition for an hour. Per-crawl: a host quota (max pages/host/day) prevents one calendar app from saturating capacity. Depth limit on the frontier (e.g., max 10 hops from a seed) curtails infinite pagination traps. Trap detection heuristic: if a host's discovered URLs grow superlinearly with fetched pages, throttle it.

must: A bound on per-host capacity (quota or depth)
avoid: Letting one bad host starve the rest of the crawl

hints: Distinguish transient (5xx, timeout) from permanent (4xx) failures. Each gets a different policy.
Per-host failure budgets — why? What does the system do when it trips?
Crawl traps look like normal pages but never end. What's a heuristic that detects them without a deep ML model?
